My fainting fit probably lasted a considerable time; for, when I recovered, it was long before I could understand my situation, or recall anything that had happened to my memory. At length, peace by peace, the truth came before me, and I could feel the cold sweat trickling down my brow. The voice I had heard echoed probably in imagination; for it was how silent. A low deep sound was humming in my ears, which I could at length distinguish to be the sinful sounds of human beings, separated from me either by distance or some thick and deadening barrier. I endeavored in vain to divide it into its component parts and to recognize the voices of those I knew; and there was something more horrible in this vague mysterious monotony than I had been sincerely fraught with; the dying accents of the one loved best on earth felt as if mine must be bitter than that of the rest. I was alone! I was cut off even from the tongues of my suitors; while they, I imagined, were together, and in the solace of one another's voices, and the touch even of one another's clothes. I received some relief from the idea of total abandonment, of agony unimagined.

My senses, I believe, began to stir; I complained aloud of my lonely fate: I knew that I was behaving absurdly; but could not help it; I beat the non walls of my dungeon with my clenched hands till they were wet with blood, and rendered terrific by horror &c. Despair. The voices of the rest appeared to be startled into silence at the sound, or perhaps it fell upon their ears like a cry of comfort and hope, an answer to their groans from the surface of the earth. After a pause I heard another dull, heavy sound. Like that produced by a muffled drum; it was in reality a drum, and half, is, a loss of it, more powerful in causing attention than his own voice. The sound, in such circumstances, was inexpressibly dull; and when the hand that smote the instrument in so unctuous scene wandered by in its regular tune, my sensations were exaggerated into spectacles of horror which I can liken only to that which might be supposed to visit a religious mind on witnessing some shocking and blasphemous event.

I may seem a species of insanity to mention it; but when the roll of the drum and the sound of human voices had ceased, and I had been left for considerable time, as I were, to myself, even in these circumstances of terror, and loneliness, and mystery, I possessed a species of knowledge to which the dull ears of the surface would have deemed equally useless and unsuitable to themselves underground. I knew the hour of the night like the idiot, marked at the proper intervals the audible measure, met at tune, after the clock was removed, which it taught him, the practice, my inclination for drinking, which had been converted by habit into an almost unconquerable passion, returned at the accustomed time of its gratification. In spite of surrounding circumstances, I found myself in the midst of my dissolute companions, in the scene of our coarse and vulgar revel, drank, but without being filled; became drunken without intoxication; and the close and poisonous atmosphere, which before had been harrumphing my groans, now rang with song, and laughter and imprecations. The state of unnatural excitement passed away, but the reactions which took place exhibited all the symptoms that attend the awakening of the young and inexperienced drunkard, with headache, sickness, fear, irritability, tremors; I awoke in a horror of great darkness.

Then the ideas, wholesome in themselves, but which in such circumstances are like daggers, crowded round my hurried and scared heart. My horror for my family, my arrogance, my ingratitude, my dishonesty, my misspent time, my forgotten duties, blasphemed and unregarded God! I buried my face in my hands, but could not hide them from my soul. Slowly and sternly they passed before me; but the last idea swallowed up its precursors, and with a star, and a shudder, found myself trembling on the verge of eternity on the very steps of the Judgment seat, entering into the presence of the awful and eternal Judge.

It would be esteemed an example of pith, when I mention next my hunger and thirst, and say that these passions, in the physical body, almost neutralized the effect of the above on my immortal soul. Hunger, indeed, may be borne, at least to an extent, but this is truly a chastisement of seriousness.

I have not described my feelings; have simply catalogued, and in very incomplete manner, their proximate causes. I sank by degrees into a sort of stupor, from which I was awakened by the light of heaven streaming in my face, through an aperture made in the roof by my deliverance. The apparent apathy, as some term in philosophy, which displayed, has been attributed to wrong causes. The truth is, that although at first my body was awake, my mind was almost wholly insensible; I recovered its consciousness by very slow degrees, and it was not until I was alone a night, that I became completely sensible of my irreverence.

We have much satisfaction in saying, that the unfortunate and imprudent young man, for whose interesting narrative we reckon confident on the thanks of our readers, is now improved to one of danger. He has been removed to the house of a friend of his father, an eminent solicitor in Gray's Inn; but even while in the hospital, he was visited by many persons of the highest responsibility. His most constant attendant, however, was a young female, who had been due of the house, almost unhurt, very soon after the accident happened. We are restrained, by considerations of delicacy, from advertising in a particular manner to her connection with the narrative; but she was the lady who stood upon the stage at the time of the accident. Miss Williams's information must have been mistaken, as to her person, for she is not Mrs. — but Miss — London Lessee Register.
